event.name: Buying and Merchandising Team Decision Making

sourceNotes: Seeded from BTDM roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: BTDM event flavor, then this event's own instructional areas, then the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Merchandise a buyer may still order for delivery inside a period: planned EOM stock + planned sales + planned reductions - BOM stock - merchandise already on order.
terms.whyItMatters: A BTDM case hands the team a month's plan and asks how much is left to spend; a team that forgets to subtract goods already on order overcommits the budget and cannot defend the number in the judge's follow-up.

terms.definition: Planned sales + planned reductions + planned EOM stock - planned BOM stock, stated at retail; a buyer converts it to cost by applying the planned initial markup before writing orders.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give four of the five figures and ask for the fifth, and roleplays ask a team to turn a retail purchase plan into the cost dollars an order sheet actually carries.

terms.definition: BOM stock = planned sales for the month + (average monthly stock - average monthly sales), so a cushion rides above expected sales; used when annual turnover runs under about six.
terms.whyItMatters: A stock-planning roleplay for a slow-turning classification such as furniture is solved with this formula, and picking it over the percentage variation method is half the judge's rubric.

terms.definition: BOM stock = average stock x 1/2 x (1 + planned month's sales / average monthly sales), which holds inventory closer to the mean than sales swing; used when turnover exceeds six.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a season plan with a heavy December, this is the method that keeps the December opening stock from doubling, and BTDM teams are scored on choosing it for fast-turning goods.

terms.definition: Stock is set at planned weekly sales x the desired weeks of cover, where the cover figure equals weeks in the period / the period's planned stock turn - 26 weeks at a 5.2 turn gives 5 weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Replenishment roleplays state a turn goal and a weekly rate of sale and ask for the on-hand target; teams that reason in dollars instead of weeks miss the unit answer the judge wants.

terms.definition: Downward price change that only reverses a previously taken additional markup and may never fall below the original retail; it nets against markups and is not reported as a markdown.
terms.whyItMatters: Classifying one of these as a markdown overstates reductions and understates maintained margin, which is exactly the trap in gross-margin reconciliation questions.

terms.definition: Extra deduction earned by paying an invoice before even the cash-discount period expires, computed as an annual rate on the days prepaid and taken on top of the cash discount.
terms.whyItMatters: A negotiation roleplay with a cash-rich retailer turns on whether the team can quantify what paying 20 days early is worth, rather than just asking for a lower price.

terms.definition: Periods are counted from the end of the invoice month, and invoices dated on or after the 25th roll to the following month - so a March 26 shipment on 2/10 EOM is still discountable May 10.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash-flow questions in a buying case ask for the exact last day a discount can be taken, and the 25th-of-the-month rule is the step teams skip.

terms.definition: One rate that replaces a series, found as 1 - (1 - d1)(1 - d2)(1 - d3): a 20/10/5 chain equals 31.6%, not the 35% a team gets by adding the three discounts together.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor quotes arrive as chains, and comparing two suppliers' offers in a roleplay is wrong the moment a team adds the percentages instead of compounding them.

terms.definition: Refund of up to 99% of the tariffs paid on imported goods that are afterwards exported or destroyed, claimed inside the statutory filing window and credited back against landed cost.
terms.whyItMatters: For a retailer re-exporting unsold import stock, recovering it changes the cost of that clearance, and case questions on import sourcing expect the 99% ceiling to be known.

terms.definition: Title, risk of loss and transportation charges all stay with the seller until goods reach the buyer's dock, so the quoted price already contains freight and the buyer files no damage claim.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing vendor quotes in a roleplay requires knowing which one bundles freight, and this term settles who claims against the carrier when a shipment arrives crushed.

terms.definition: Ratio of what the goods available cost to what they are ticketed at — $520,000 against $1,000,000 of retail gives 0.52 — and multiplying an ending retail book figure by it converts that inventory to cost without counting a ticket.
terms.whyItMatters: A buying case that states purchases at both cost and retail asks for the cost value of closing stock, and a team that averages the markup percentages instead of dividing the two totals reports a number the judge can disprove in one line.

terms.definition: Season-to-date markup on everything handled — (total retail of goods available minus their total cost) divided by that total retail — so one off-price buy taken at 60% lifts the running figure above the 48% planned on the opening order.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges ask what markup the rest of the season's buys must carry, and that answer is computed from the running figure on all goods handled, never from the markup written on the last purchase order.

terms.definition: Working out what the unbought balance must carry to reach plan: subtract the retail already committed from the planned total retail, subtract the cost already committed from the planned total cost, then divide — $6,000 of cost taken at 40% against a $10,000 cost plan at 50% forces 60% on the rest.
terms.whyItMatters: When a vendor offers a mid-season closeout at a thin markup, the roleplay asks whether the team can still hit plan; the defensible answer is the markup the balance would then have to carry and whether the market will bear it.

terms.definition: Beginning-of-month inventory divided by that month's planned sales — a 4.0 means opening with four retail dollars for every dollar planned to sell, and the reciprocal of the ratio is that month's turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: Season plans hand a team the ratio by month plus the sales plan, and the opening stock line is the product of the two; multiplying by the wrong month's ratio misplans every receipt after it.

terms.definition: Units a reduced price must move to hold the same gross-margin dollars: old units times old unit margin, divided by the new unit margin — a $40 item costing $20 cut to $32 keeps $12, so it takes 1.67 sales to replace each one before.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay whether to take 20% off slow goods, the team that states how much faster the item must sell to stay whole beats the team that only quotes the markdown percentage.

terms.definition: The figure a retail price is actually built on: list less each trade discount applied in sequence, then the cash discount on that result, then vendor allowances, with inbound freight added back — the deductions never share one base.
terms.whyItMatters: Two vendor quotes in a buying roleplay are only comparable at this number, and a team that stops at invoice cost sets a retail that quietly misses the planned initial markup.

terms.definition: The discount clock starts the day the goods arrive rather than the day the invoice is written, so 2/10 ROG on an order spending six weeks on the water is still discountable ten days after the container is unloaded.
terms.whyItMatters: Import buying roleplays ask which terms protect cash flow on a long transit, and this is the concession to negotiate when ordinary end-of-month terms would lapse before the shipment lands.

terms.definition: Title passes to the retailer and the goods sit on its books, but unsold units may be returned by an agreed date — unlike consignment, where the vendor keeps title and is paid only after each sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Bringing in an unproven brand, a team must say who carries the markdown risk and whose balance sheet holds the inventory; the judge's rubric splits on exactly that line.

terms.definition: Price quoted at the overseas factory gate, before agent commission, inland haulage, ocean freight, insurance and duty are stacked onto it — it equals landed cost only in a quote that already bundles every one of those.
terms.whyItMatters: A sourcing roleplay sets an overseas quote against a domestic one, and a team that compares this figure to a delivered domestic price recommends the wrong vendor by a wide margin.

terms.definition: Duty is assessed on the price actually paid for the goods themselves, so international freight and insurance stay outside the base while packing charges, royalties and buyer-supplied assists are added into it.
terms.whyItMatters: Landed-cost questions ask for the duty dollars, not the rate, and a team that multiplies the rate by the full delivered cost overstates the tariff and misprices the whole order.

terms.definition: Tooling, molds, materials or design work the buyer hands an overseas factory free or below cost; its value is apportioned across the units produced and added to the customs value even though no money changed hands at entry.
terms.whyItMatters: A team sourcing a private-label program that ships its own molds to the plant must apportion that value into the entry, or the duty underpayment surfaces when the entry is liquidated months later.

terms.definition: A lower rate applies only to the first block of units admitted in the quota year, and everything clearing after that block pays a much higher rate — so identical orders land at two different costs depending on arrival date.
terms.whyItMatters: Deciding whether to pull a delivery earlier in a sourcing roleplay turns on whether the quota fills first, which moves landed cost per unit enough to change the retail price.

terms.definition: Goods sit on domestic soil but outside customs territory: duty is deferred until they enter commerce, avoided entirely on anything re-exported, and where the finished item's rate is lower than its components', the importer may elect that lower rate.
terms.whyItMatters: For import stock held months before release, the deferred duty is real working capital, and a case asking how to cut import carrying cost expects this rather than a bigger order.

terms.definition: Units a fixture needs to look shopable and that therefore never sell — four per door across 60 doors ties up 240 units of the buy before a single one is available to a customer.
terms.whyItMatters: A team that buys 300 units for a 60-door rollout finds only 60 are truly sellable, and allocation roleplays are scored on catching that arithmetic before the order is written.

terms.definition: Splitting a short receipt by each store's share of forecast demand instead of evenly — a door forecast at 8% of the chain draws 8% of the units, so 1,000 units send 80 there and no volume door is starved.
terms.whyItMatters: When a hot item arrives short, the judge asks how the team divides it across doors, and an equal split is the answer that loses the decision.

terms.definition: Reorder fires when on-hand falls to the minimum, and the quantity ordered is the maximum less on-hand less whatever is already on order — skip that last subtraction and the same need is bought twice.
terms.whyItMatters: Basic-goods replenishment roleplays hand a team on-hand and on-order figures and ask for the order quantity; ignoring the open orders is the standard error the rubric watches for.

terms.definition: Planned purchases turn negative once orders already written are subtracted, meaning the period's money is committed before it opens — leaving only cancellation, pushing deliveries into the next period, or planning added reductions.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that hands a team a fully committed budget plus a tempting new vendor offer is testing whether they name the position and a remedy instead of asking for more money.

terms.definition: The order size at which a vendor's next discount tier makes the bigger buy genuinely cheaper: the tier's saving has to beat the cost of carrying the extra weeks of supply it creates, not merely lower the unit price.
terms.whyItMatters: Offered a better price at double the quantity, the team that prices the carrying cost of that extra cover can defend either decision; the team reading only the unit price always buys.

terms.definition: Annual percentage of inventory value eaten by tied-up capital, storage, insurance, obsolescence and damage — commonly around a quarter of value, so an extra thirteen weeks of cover costs roughly 6% of what those goods cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Every buy-deeper-for-a-better-price offer in a buying roleplay is settled by whether the discount beats this rate across the extra weeks of supply it forces the retailer to hold.

terms.definition: Order value at which a vendor stops billing transportation, which makes the last dollars of an order the cheapest — adding $400 to clear a $5,000 threshold can save $300 of freight, but only on goods the plan actually wanted.
terms.whyItMatters: Order-writing questions ask whether to round an order up to the threshold, and the answer has to weigh the freight saved against inventory the open-to-buy never planned.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: Helping customers make purchase decisions through planned communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling vocabulary supports recommendations about staff, service, and revenue.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: The path a product takes from producer or provider to the final customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel choices affect convenience, cost, access, and customer experience.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: Deals won divided by every qualified opportunity worked in the period — 15 wins out of 60 qualified opportunities is 25%. The denominator keeps opportunities that are still open or that ended in no decision, which is exactly what win rate throws out, so this figure always reads lower than win rate for the same rep.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales-management roleplay that asks you to diagnose a rep whose revenue is falling, a dropping close rate against a steady win rate points at unqualified prospecting rather than weak closing technique.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: An intermediary that helps buy or sell on a producer's behalf without taking title to goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Agents lower channel cost by handling transactions without holding inventory.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: The structured steps that move a customer from awareness to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the process helps competitors execute each stage well.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: A distribution path where a producer sells straight to customers with no intermediaries.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct channels maximize control and margin but demand more sales and logistics effort.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: Deals won divided only by the deals that reached a final decision — wins plus losses — so 15 wins among 45 resolved deals is 33%, with open and no-decision opportunities excluded from the denominator entirely. That narrower denominator is the whole difference from close rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that hand you a pipeline table expect you to notice which opportunities belong in the denominator; counting still-open deals as losses is the single most common wrong answer.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: The drop in required buyer-seller contacts when an intermediary is inserted: 5 producers selling to 20 retailers need 5 x 20 = 100 direct contacts, but routing through one wholesaler needs only 5 + 20 = 25. The M x N to M + N shift, not friendliness of service, is the economic justification for paying an intermediary a margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A distribution roleplay that asks you to defend adding a wholesaler is scored on whether you can produce the contact math; judges reject the vague answer that a middleman 'saves time.'

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: Identifying and qualifying potential customers who may need an offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective prospecting builds the foundation for successful sales.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: Friction between firms at the SAME stage of a channel — two franchisees of one brand advertising into each other's trade area, or two dealers discounting against each other. Vertical channel conflict, by contrast, runs between DIFFERENT stages: a manufacturer and its distributor fighting over margin or over the manufacturer's own web store.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-management roleplay hands you an angry dealer and asks for a fix; the remedy differs by type — territory rules settle horizontal disputes, margin or policy changes settle vertical ones.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: Open opportunity value divided by the quota for the period: $900,000 of open deals against a $300,000 quota is 3x, the usual rule of thumb for a team that wins about one deal in three. Coverage below the reciprocal of the win rate means the quota is arithmetically unreachable no matter how well the rep sells.
terms.whyItMatters: A district-manager roleplay judged on forecasting expects you to test coverage before promising a number, and to prescribe prospecting rather than closing coaching when coverage is thin.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: A distribution path where one or more intermediaries sit between producer and customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Indirect channels widen reach and share costs but reduce producer control.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: The opening contact and strategy used to engage a potential customer.
terms.whyItMatters: A professional approach sets the first impression that drives interest.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: Two firms at the SAME channel stage pooling capital, production or distribution to chase an opportunity neither could take alone — a coffee brand operating kiosks inside a bookstore chain. A vertical marketing system, by contrast, joins firms at DIFFERENT stages of the same channel under one owner, contract or dominant member.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship and marketing roleplays that propose a co-branded partnership are graded on naming this structure and the fact that neither partner is the other's supplier.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: Number of open opportunities multiplied by average deal size multiplied by win rate, all divided by the average sales cycle length in days, which yields revenue per day: 50 x $4,000 x 0.30 / 60 days = $1,000 a day. It is the one common metric where shortening the cycle raises revenue without adding a single new prospect.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks which of four fixes lifts revenue fastest, the velocity formula shows that cutting cycle time is a divisor change and beats a small win-rate gain.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: One member's ability to make another do what it otherwise would not, drawn from the five French-and-Raven bases: coercive (threatening to cut supply or shelf space), reward (extra margin or funds), expert (knowledge the other lacks), referent (the partner wants the association), and legitimate (a contract already requires it). Coercive power gets compliance but raises conflict; referent and expert power get cooperation.
terms.whyItMatters: A channel-relationship roleplay asks how you would move a resistant distributor; naming the base you are using, and why coercion would cost you the relationship, is the scored discrimination.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: The portion of total addressable demand a firm's product, price point and channels can actually reach — the total narrowed to the segments and geographies it serves. Narrow it once more by the share realistically winnable in the plan period and you have the serviceable obtainable market.
terms.whyItMatters: Written-event plans that state one giant industry figure lose points; judges expect the total narrowed twice, with the reason for each cut named.

terms.definition: Asking questions to understand a customer's problems, goals, and requirements.
terms.whyItMatters: Assessing needs ensures recommendations truly solve the customer's problem.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: A business between producer and customer, such as a retailer, wholesaler, or agent.
terms.whyItMatters: Intermediaries expand reach but add cost and control tradeoffs.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: Units of a specific add-on sold divided by units of the primary product sold, times 100 — 300 protection plans on 1,000 phones is 30%. It scores one named pairing, where cross-sell measurement counts every additional category a customer buys, so a store can raise total cross-sell revenue while this figure falls.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays that set an accessories goal are graded on whether you name the ratio you will move and the counter behavior that moves it, not on a general promise to sell more.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: Selling across store, web, app and marketplace on ONE shared inventory pool, price and customer record, so a shopper can start a purchase in one place and finish it in another. The test that separates it from multichannel is integration: multichannel runs each channel as a separate P&L with its own stock and pricing, so an order begun online cannot be returned or completed in the store.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and marketing roleplays ask you to fix a customer who bought online and was refused a store return — the answer names the missing integration, not better staff training.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: A product's characteristics and the value those characteristics give.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must separate features from benefits to sell effectively.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: An intermediary that buys goods in bulk from producers and resells them to retailers.
terms.whyItMatters: Wholesalers aggregate inventory and provide the logistics that enable retail networks.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: A six-part qualification framework — Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion — that adds the buyer's internal mechanics, the written criteria and the approval path, to the money-and-authority checks BANT stops at. It is built for long committee purchases where the signer is never the first contact.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business roleplay with a committee, naming the economic buyer and the decision criteria is the specific step judges look for before any presentation content.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: Splitting the work of a SINGLE sale across different members — the customer configures and orders online, a local dealer installs and services, and the manufacturer invoices. It differs from dual distribution, where two COMPLETE channels each handle a whole sale end to end and therefore compete with each other for the same order.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selection roleplays for a product needing installation are scored on assigning each channel function to whoever performs it best rather than choosing one channel outright.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: A method built on teach, tailor and take control, in which the rep opens with a commercial insight that reframes how the buyer sees their own business and then respectfully pushes back on the buyer's assumptions. Relationship selling does the reverse: it builds trust first and delivers whatever the buyer already says they want.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judged on demonstrating expertise rewards teaching the buyer something about their own market, while a purely agreeable rep reads as an order taker.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: A producer moving the same product through two channels that compete for the same buyer — company-owned stores alongside independent dealers, or a factory site priced against its own retail accounts. Courts judge the resulting squeeze on dealers under the rule of reason rather than treating it as automatically unlawful, so the legal exposure comes from how the two channels are priced, not from having both.
terms.whyItMatters: A distribution roleplay that adds a direct web store to an existing dealer network is graded on anticipating the dealer revolt and proposing price or territory rules that keep the arrangement defensible.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: Connecting a product feature to the benefit the customer receives.
terms.whyItMatters: It turns product facts into customer value.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: A strategy to make a product available in as many outlets as possible.
terms.whyItMatters: It maximizes convenience and market penetration for high-demand goods.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: An advance paid to a rep against commission not yet earned — a $3,000 monthly draw against $2,200 of earnings leaves $800 outstanding. A recoverable draw carries that $800 forward against next month's commissions, while a non-recoverable draw forgives it, which makes the second version a guaranteed minimum in everything but name.
terms.whyItMatters: Human-resources and selling exam items ask which pay plan protects a new rep during a long ramp, and the recoverable-versus-non-recoverable distinction is the answer's hinge.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: GENUINE branded products sold through a channel the trademark owner never authorized, usually diverted from a market where the wholesale price was lower. They are lawful to resell in the United States because the first-sale doctrine exhausts the owner's control over that particular unit; counterfeit goods differ absolutely — those are fake, and selling them is trademark infringement no matter who bought them first.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-considerations items in channel management hinge on this split: a competitor undercutting an authorized dealer with real goods is generally legal, and the manufacturer's remedy is contractual, not a lawsuit for infringement.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: A structured pitch showing how an offering meets the customer's needs.
terms.whyItMatters: A compelling presentation moves a prospect toward purchase.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: Buying a producer's goods legitimately in a low-price country and importing them for resale below the authorized dealer's price at home. The Supreme Court's 2013 ruling in Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons held that the first-sale doctrine covers copies lawfully made abroad, so the importer wins on copyright grounds and the producer's only real defenses are contract terms with its foreign distributors and genuine material differences in the product.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethical- and legal-consideration questions in channel management use this case to separate what a manufacturer dislikes from what it can actually stop.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: A higher commission rate applied only to revenue above quota — 8% up to plan and 12% beyond it — so each dollar of overperformance pays more than the first dollar did. A cap or a decelerator does the reverse and is precisely what tempts a rep to hold a signed deal until the next period opens.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on motivating a sales force ask which plan change stops sandbagging at quarter end, and the rate structure above quota is the mechanism being tested.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: Selling through a limited number of carefully chosen intermediaries in an area.
terms.whyItMatters: It balances accessibility with brand control and partner profitability.

terms.definition: Puts a written or drawn description of an unbuilt product before target buyers and scores stated purchase intent, normally reading the top two boxes of a 5-point scale -- 'definitely' plus 'probably would buy' -- then discounting that figure, because stated intent runs far above actual trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Feasibility roleplays ask how you would test an idea before building it; naming the intent scale and the discount separates a real answer from 'ask some customers.'

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: Responding to a customer's concerns in a helpful, persuasive way.
terms.whyItMatters: Handling objections improves trust and conversion.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: Codified at 17 U.S.C. section 109(a): once a copyright owner authorizes the first sale of a particular copy, its distribution right in THAT copy is exhausted, so the buyer may resell, rent or give it away without permission. Exhaustion covers distribution only — the reproduction right survives, so reselling a book is protected while photocopying it is not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the rule behind resale markets, used bookstores and outlet diverters, and channel exams test whether you know a manufacturer cannot use copyright to block resale of units it already sold.

terms.definition: Laws and rules ensuring fair practices and safeguarding customer rights.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding it helps a business operate ethically and avoid liability.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: Sizing territories by the work each contains: accounts multiplied by the calls per year each requires, divided by the calls one rep can make — 400 accounts needing 12 calls each is 4,800 calls, and at 800 calls per rep that is six territories. The breakdown method instead divides a sales forecast by average revenue per rep and ignores how much service each account demands.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay asking you to rebalance territories after a merger wants the calculation and the service load, not an even split of the map.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: Appointing only one or a few intermediaries to sell in a territory.
terms.whyItMatters: It gives partners strong incentives and control, ideal for premium products.

terms.definition: A pre-release trial run by the developer's own employees inside a controlled company setting, so defects are found before any outsider sees the product; beta testing hands the same build to real customers in their own environment, which makes who runs it and where the dividing line between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: Development-stage exam items list a testing activity and ask which stage it belongs to; the answer turns entirely on whether outsiders are involved.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: Asking for the order or finalizing the agreement to complete the sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing when and how to close prevents lost opportunities.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: An independent business that BUYS the goods, holds title, and therefore carries inventory risk, obsolescence and the credit exposure on resale, earning a margin rather than a fee. Agents and brokers sit on the other side of that line: they never take title, never bear the inventory risk, and are paid a commission — commonly 2 to 7 percent of the sale — for arranging the transaction.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a distribution partner and ask which type it is; the deciding fact is always whether title passed, and title decides who eats unsold stock.

terms.definition: The specific benefit that makes a product distinctly better than rivals'.
terms.whyItMatters: A clear USP gives customers a compelling reason to choose the product.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: The Federal Trade Commission provision giving a buyer until midnight of the third business day to cancel a sale of $25 or more made at their home or anywhere other than the seller's permanent place of business, with the seller required to hand over two dated cancellation forms at signing. Sales made inside the seller's own store are not covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal and ethical selling items on the exam test the dollar threshold and the location condition, and in-home roleplays expect you to disclose the cancellation right rather than hurry the signature.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: A paid matchmaker who brings a buyer and seller together for ONE transaction, takes neither title nor physical possession, and has no ongoing representation of either side once the deal closes. A manufacturers' representative differs on exactly that point: it works under a continuing contract for a defined territory and product line, calling on the same accounts year after year.
terms.whyItMatters: Food, real-estate and insurance channel scenarios turn on this: a broker cannot promise delivery terms or warranty support because it never owned the goods and has no standing agency.

terms.definition: The first 2.5% of a market to buy something new -- venturesome, able to absorb a failed purchase, and often socially outside the mainstream, which limits their influence; the early adopters who follow are the next 13.5% and carry the opinion leadership that actually moves the majority.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target at launch; quoting the 2.5% band and then explaining why that group cannot spread adoption alone is what separates the top scores.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: Recommending additional products based on the customer's current purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Suggestive selling raises transaction value and meets more needs.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Disagreement between channel members over goals, territories, or profits.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict damages efficiency; resolving it is key to long-term channel health.

terms.definition: The 13.5% of buyers who follow the innovators -- respected opinion leaders inside the mainstream whose endorsement decides whether an item reaches the 34% early majority; innovators, the first 2.5%, buy sooner but sit too far outside the group to persuade it.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion plans for a launch are scored on targeting the group that others watch; naming the 13.5% band and its opinion-leader role answers the indicator directly.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: Exaggerated subjective praise no reasonable buyer would treat as fact — the finest coffee in town — which creates no liability, as opposed to a misrepresentation, a specific factual claim about performance, condition or origin that does. The dividing test is whether the statement could be proven false.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethical selling roleplays plant a tempting overstatement, and knowing that this machine will cut your costs in half is a checkable claim while our machines are the best is not keeps you on the right side of the rubric.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: A merchant wholesaler that owns the merchandise sitting on a retailer's fixture, chooses the assortment, sets the planogram, restocks on its own route, and is paid only for units that actually scan — so the retailer risks nothing but the floor space. A conventional wholesaler is the opposite arrangement: it bills the retailer at delivery and the retailer owns the unsold goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Convenience-store, greeting-card and paperback scenarios use this to test who bears shrink and markdown risk when the supplier still owns the stock on the shelf.

terms.definition: Measures how closely the lines relate in production, distribution, and end use -- something neither width nor depth can show: two firms each carrying 4 lines and 40 items differ sharply when one sells only refrigerated foods through grocers and the other sells food, tires, and insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification questions ask whether a proposed line fits; the scoring point is that the new line shares plants or channels with the existing ones, not that it sounds related.

terms.definition: How a product or brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning shapes differentiation and appeal to the target market.

terms.definition: A seller's factual affirmation, description, sample or model that becomes part of the basis of the bargain, created by the statement itself with no formal words and no intent required — where an implied warranty arises automatically from the sale by operation of law. A rep quoting a performance figure in a presentation can create one without meaning to.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling exam items ask which of four salesperson statements creates a binding promise, and the answer is always the specific, checkable one rather than the general praise beside it.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: A wholesaler that TAKES TITLE to a shipment but never physically handles it — it sells the load, then instructs the producer to ship straight to the buyer, collecting the margin between the two prices. That title-without-possession position is what separates it from a broker, which never takes title at all, and from a full-service wholesaler, which warehouses and delivers the goods itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Bulk-commodity channel questions test whether you see that this member is legally the seller of record and therefore liable on the sale, even though it never touched the freight.

terms.definition: A purchase for which buyers accept no substitute and will pass closer outlets to reach one brand -- insistence, not preference; a shopping good is one buyers compare on price, quality, and style across several stores and will happily switch brands on to save money.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution questions follow from this classification: specialty goods justify exclusive distribution and few outlets, while shopping goods need enough outlets for comparison to happen.

terms.definition: Two towns pull trade from the countryside between them in proportion to their populations and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to each; the indifference line sits at the miles between them ÷ (1 + the square root of the larger town's population divided by the smaller town's), measured out from the smaller town, and households past that line shop the larger one.
terms.whyItMatters: A trading-area item on the marketing exam gives two populations and the miles between the towns and expects the boundary mileage as a number; in a site-selection roleplay it is how you defend where a store stops drawing customers instead of waving at a map.

terms.definition: Developing a base of regular customers who return to buy again.
terms.whyItMatters: A strong clientele provides stable revenue and drives growth.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: A non-competing business that partners to offer complementary products to shared customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Affinity partnerships extend reach and value without adding intermediaries.

terms.definition: Moves a new product through fixed stages separated by go/kill reviews with written criteria, so a project can die at any gate -- screening, business analysis, development, testing, launch; the long-standing planning ratio is roughly 7 serious ideas entering for every 1 commercial success.
terms.whyItMatters: Development roleplays ask what happens between an idea and a launch; the scoring point is that each gate can kill the project, not that the stages happen in order.

terms.definition: Estimates the probability a shopper in a neighborhood picks one particular store as that store's selling area ÷ travel time raised to a decay exponent (commonly 2), divided by the same ratio summed across every competing store; multiplying that probability by neighborhood households and their annual category spending turns it into a sales forecast for the site.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-comparison questions that ask which of three locations captures the most volume are solved by ranking size-over-distance-squared ratios, and unlike a single breaking-point line this one gives every store a share of every neighborhood — the distinction a judge probes.

terms.definition: Share of one cohort of leads that becomes a qualified opportunity: opportunities created divided by the leads that entered in that same period, never by every lead sitting in the database. 40 opportunities from 500 new leads is 8 percent; dividing by a 12,000-record database reports 0.3 percent and hides the follow-up problem entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel-math items hand you a month of lead counts and opportunity counts and grade the denominator you pick, and a roleplay on tracking prospecting results expects the rate quoted per period rather than against the whole list.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Performs the whole function set — carries inventory, extends trade credit, delivers, fields a sales force, and merchandises the account — and prices for it, typically working on a 15 to 25 percent gross margin. A limited-service wholesaler strips some of those out (cash-and-carry drops credit and delivery, a truck jobber drops credit) and consequently operates nearer 8 to 12 percent.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-cost questions ask why one supplier quotes a higher landed price than another; the answer is the bundle of functions inside the margin, not inefficiency.

terms.definition: Portable, shorter-lived business goods bought routinely by middle managers and written off over a few years -- hand tools, laptops, forklifts; an installation is the major capital asset such as a plant or a production line, approved by top management on a multi-year capital budget.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business selling roleplays are scored on calling on the right buyer: the pair differs by who signs, so pitching an installation to a department manager is a scoring miss.

terms.definition: A distinctive strength that lets a business outperform its competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Naming the advantage shapes marketing messages and differentiation.

terms.definition: The emotional and rational reasons a customer makes a purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding motives helps position products around what matters.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: The management of the flow of goods — storage, transportation, and delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: Logistics efficiency drives channel cost, speed, and customer satisfaction.

terms.definition: Applies stated go/no-go criteria to drop weak concepts before money is spent, and guards against two opposite errors -- a drop-error that kills a winner and a go-error that carries a loser into costly development; idea generation, by contrast, deliberately withholds all judgment to maximize the count.
terms.whyItMatters: A brainstorming roleplay is scored badly if you evaluate while generating; competitors must say which stage they are in and which error that stage is trying to avoid.

terms.definition: Weights availability by the share of category dollar volume rung up in the stores that stock an item rather than the share of stores stocking it: 400 supermarkets out of 2,000 can be 65% ACV when they are the busiest 400, so an item in a fifth of outlets can still stand in front of two-thirds of category purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution items hand a store count alongside a volume weighting and expect the weighted figure; a marketing-plan roleplay that claims 'we reach most of the market' collapses when the judge asks which of the two numbers that claim rests on.

terms.definition: Total quota handed out across the sales force divided by the revenue the company actually forecasts. Assigning 1.1 to 1.3 times the target is deliberate over-assignment that absorbs ramping reps, mid-year attrition and under-performers, so the plan still lands if some reps miss — it measures quota against target, where pipeline coverage measures open deals against quota.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay that asks you to set quotas for next year is scored on whether you over-assign on purpose and can say why; the exam pairs this with pipeline coverage to see if you can tell the two ratios apart.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: An independent salesperson carrying several producers' NON-COMPETING lines in a defined territory on commission of roughly 5 to 15 percent of net sales, with no title to the goods and no authority to set price or terms. A selling agent is the stronger form: it contracts for a producer's ENTIRE output and does hold authority over price, terms and promotion, effectively acting as that producer's marketing department.
terms.whyItMatters: A start-up roleplay choosing between hiring salespeople and appointing reps is graded on the fixed-versus-variable cost trade and on who controls pricing under each arrangement.

terms.definition: A finished business good that goes into another product and keeps its own identity there -- a car battery, a tire, a microchip; raw materials are processed until that identity is lost, and maintenance and repair supplies never enter the finished product at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Industrial product questions ask you to classify an input; the identity test decides it, and it also explains why component makers can advertise to the end consumer at all.

terms.definition: Counts the plain percentage of outlets in the defined universe that stock an item — 400 of 2,000 stores is 20% — and says nothing about how much those outlets sell; dividing weighted (%ACV) coverage by this number gives a quality-of-distribution ratio that runs above 1.0 when the item sits in the bigger stores and below it when the item is stranded in small ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-choice questions supply both coverage figures and ask which distribution plan is stronger; the ratio between them is the answer, and treating the two numbers as interchangeable is the classic miss on that item.

terms.definition: Closed-won revenue divided by the number of deals won — $480,000 across 60 wins is $8,000 each. It measures one whole customer agreement, where average order value measures one transaction, so a customer who reorders four times a year raises order count without raising this figure at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking you to justify spending more selling time per account is answered by comparing deal size against cost per sales call, not by citing total revenue.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: A recurring fee the franchisee owes on GROSS SALES, not profit — commonly 4 to 8 percent — plus a separate advertising-fund contribution of about 1 to 3 percent, both paid on top of a one-time initial fee. Because the base is revenue, the fee is owed in full in a month the outlet loses money, which is the fact most competitors miss.
terms.whyItMatters: Franchise roleplays that ask whether a location can carry its costs are scored on running the royalty off sales; treating it as a share of profit produces the wrong break-even every time.

terms.definition: Places a pre-release version with outside customers doing real work in their own conditions, capturing failures no internal lab reproduces; alpha testing comes first and is run in-house by employees, so a beta's whole value is the uncontrolled use an alpha deliberately excludes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a limited launch is scored on why outside users are needed before full production, not merely on saying the product will be tested.

terms.definition: The specific actions and tools used to carry out a marketing strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Tactics turn strategy into concrete, executable actions.

terms.definition: Every open deal multiplied by the win probability its current stage carries, then summed. A $200,000 deal sitting in a 30 percent stage counts as $60,000, so $1.4 million of raw pipeline spread across early stages may weight to under $400,000 — the total becomes a forecast instead of a list of what is theoretically in play.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting items give a table of deal values and stage probabilities and expect the weighted total, not the sum; in a roleplay defending a forecast to a manager, quoting raw pipeline reads as the rookie answer.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Each independent layer that performs negotiation work or takes title on the way from producer to end user. A zero-level channel is producer straight to consumer; a broker or agent counts as a level even though it never owns the goods, while carriers, banks and public warehouses count as none because they never negotiate terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a shipping diagram and ask how many levels it has; the trap is counting the trucking firm, which never negotiates and therefore adds no level.

terms.definition: The contract section fixing measurable performance targets and the credit owed when they are missed: 99.9% monthly uptime allows roughly 43 minutes of outage in a 30-day month, and each tier missed below that refunds a stated percentage of the month's fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-services roleplays ask what the client is actually promised; converting a percentage into allowed minutes and naming the credit is what makes the promise enforceable.

terms.definition: Divides a brand's sales by its %ACV coverage so brands with unequal shelf presence can be compared on equal footing: $2,000,000 on 40% ACV is $50,000 per point and beats $3,000,000 on 90% ACV at $33,333 per point, which says the smaller brand has earned more distribution rather than more advertising.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-plan defense that has to say where the next dollar goes is decided by which brand turns each point of coverage into the most volume; the exam version simply hands sales and coverage and asks for the per-point figure.

terms.definition: Purchase price plus installation, training, consumables, maintenance and downtime across the asset's life, minus its resale value — so a $12,000 machine burning $400 of supplies a year beats a $9,000 machine burning $1,600 within five years. It answers a price objection by moving the comparison from acquisition price to lifetime cost.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer says a competitor quoted less, judges look for this calculation rather than a discount, because conceding on price is the response the rubric marks down.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: A supplier's promise not to appoint another reseller inside a defined area — a radius, a ZIP-code set, or a named account list — in exchange for the dealer's investment in stock, demo space and trained staff. Since Continental T.V. v. GTE Sylvania in 1977, such non-price vertical restraints are judged under the rule of reason rather than being automatically unlawful, so they stand unless they measurably harm competition among brands.
terms.whyItMatters: A distributor-agreement roleplay asks what the dealer gets for a large stocking commitment; naming the restraint and its rule-of-reason treatment is the legal-considerations point judges look for.

terms.definition: Scores quality as perception minus expectation on paired 22-item scales across five dimensions -- reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness -- so a dimension scoring 0 means expectations were met exactly and every negative number is a measured shortfall to fix.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how you would measure service quality is scored on the subtraction: measuring satisfaction alone cannot tell an over-promise from an under-delivery.

terms.definition: Measurable population traits such as age, income, education, and location.
terms.whyItMatters: Demographics let a business tailor marketing to specific segments.

terms.definition: Ramped headcount times individual quota times the attainment rate the team really achieves — 20 reps carrying $500,000 each but hitting 70 percent supports $7 million of revenue, not the $10 million the quota sheet implies. Skipping the attainment factor is what makes a hiring plan promise revenue the team has never once delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: A growth-planning roleplay that asks how many reps to hire to reach a revenue goal is graded on multiplying in historical attainment; the exam tests it as a three-factor calculation.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: A contract barring a reseller from carrying RIVAL suppliers' lines at all, which Section 3 of the Clayton Act reaches when the effect may be to substantially lessen competition.
